passage: Suraj, it's Chandrika. You asked why I took those days off last year, so here's the honest version. Every month, for years, the pain kept me on the bathroom floor, and for a few days my mood would crash so hard I'd pick fights with Arun over nothing and then cry for hours. I missed two big presentations. My aunts said, "All women bear it, beti. Drink something hot and get on with it." So I did, until the day I couldn't get out of bed for my own birthday lunch. Arun didn't argue. He just sat with me and said, "This isn't normal to live with. Let's see a doctor." The gynaecologist listened to everything, didn't once say I was exaggerating, and we made a plan. It isn't magic, but the months are manageable now. Being taken seriously shouldn't be a favour. It's a right.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's aunts tell her?
qa.a: "All women bear it, beti. Drink something hot and get on with it."

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel about the months before seeing the doctor?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and worn down, crying for hours and picking fights, while being told to just bear it.

qa.q: What was the wise response, and why?
qa.a: Seeing a doctor who listened and made a plan, because pain and mood that disrupt work and relationships deserve care, not tolerance.

qa.q: How was Arun affected, and how did he respond?
qa.a: He was drawn into fights over nothing, but instead of arguing he sat with Chandrika and suggested seeing a doctor.

grounding: Shows someone whose monthly pain and mood crashes disrupt work and relationships getting a doctor's attention instead of being told to tolerate it.

passage: I'm Bhupen, and I share a flat with my older sister Pooja. For most of the month she's the one who organises everyone. But for a few days each month something changes. She calls in sick, stays under the blanket, snaps at me for breathing loudly and then apologises in tears. Her fiancé has started asking me if he's done something wrong. I can't see inside her head. Last month, though, she told me the low felt so heavy it frightened her. I sat down next to her right then and stayed. Before she went to sleep that night, we rang her doctor's clinic together, and they gave her an appointment for the next morning. The doctor took it seriously and made a plan with her. Pooja says the worst part was believing she just had to put up with it.

qa.q: Who is worried he has upset Pooja?
qa.a: Pooja's fiancé.

qa.q: What does Pooja's crying apology suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and ashamed, unable to control the snapping and sorry for it.

qa.q: Which of Bhupen's steps was most important, and why?
qa.a: Staying with her as soon as she said the low frightened her and calling the doctor's clinic together that same night, because distress that heavy needs care at once.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see what happens to Pooja each month?
qa.a: Bhupen sees a big change that cannot be fully understood from outside, and realises it is too much for her to simply put up with.

grounding: Illustrates monthly mood and distress becoming overwhelming and disruptive, and a sibling making sure it gets a doctor's attention the same day.

passage:
January: For the week before her period, Pooja felt like a different person: exhausted, raging at small things, crying in the office washroom. Her aunt said, "Every woman goes through it. Tolerate it."
February: The week came again, heavier. One night Pooja told her sister Devika, in a flat voice, that she'd had thoughts that everyone would be better off without her. Devika sat down beside her at once, held her hand, and said, "Thank you for telling me. We're calling someone now." They rang a mental health helpline together, and Devika slept in Pooja's room that night.
March: Pooja sat in a doctor's office with Devika beside her and a diary of her symptoms. The doctor listened, took it seriously, and they made a plan together. The March week was still hard. But it was no longer something she had to tolerate alone.

qa.q: What did Pooja bring to the doctor's office?
qa.a: A diary of her symptoms.

qa.a: She thanked Pooja for telling her, stayed with her, rang a helpline together that same night, and then went with her to the doctor.

grounding: Shows overwhelming monthly distress with very dark thoughts being taken seriously the same night and then brought to a doctor, rather than tolerated.

passage: Eshaan, you asked me how to help Disha when her monthly week gets this bad. Sit, and I'll tell you about me. When I was twenty-five, before Disha was born, I had a week every month when I couldn't stop crying, couldn't sleep, and screamed at my husband over a spoon on the floor. Our old family doctor said, "It's women's nature. Bear it." I bore it for four years. I nearly lost my job at the post office, and my marriage hung by a thread. Then a young lady doctor came to the dispensary. She asked me to describe everything, wrote it all down, and said, "This is real, and there is help." That sentence saved me. So don't tell Disha to bear it, beta. Go with her to the doctor. Your Kamla Mummy is telling you from experience.

qa.q: Where did Kamla work?
qa.a: At the post office.

qa.q: How was young Kamla feeling during her bad week each month?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed and exhausted, unable to stop crying or sleep, and snapping over small things.

qa.q: What turning point helped Kamla?
qa.a: A young doctor who listened, wrote everything down and said it was real and there was help, instead of telling her to bear it.

qa.q: How did the old family doctor see Kamla's distress?
qa.a: He dismissed it as women's nature, something to be endured.

grounding: Shows that severe monthly distress disrupting work and marriage deserves a doctor's attention, and that being taken seriously is a right.

passage: The product launch was on Friday, the monsoon had flooded half of Mumbai, and Zoya was curled on the sofa with the kind of pain that made her sick. It had been getting worse every month: two days off work, snapping at Chetan, sobbing over emails she couldn't finish. Since school she had been told to put up with it. "I'll just push through and log in," she muttered. Chetan knelt beside her. "You said last month you'd see someone if it happened again. This is again." The trains had stopped, so he booked a video consultation with a gynaecologist for that afternoon and, with her nod, messaged her manager: "Zoya is unwell and seeing a doctor today; she'll update tomorrow." The doctor listened for twenty minutes, didn't tell her to tolerate it, and booked tests for the next week. Zoya cried, but this time from relief.

qa.q: Why couldn't they go to a clinic in person?
qa.a: The trains had stopped because of the flooding.

qa.q: What did Zoya feel after the doctor's call?
qa.a: She cried from relief at being taken seriously after years of being told to put up with it.

qa.q: What made Chetan's response supportive?
qa.a: He reminded Zoya of her own plan, arranged a doctor the same day despite the floods, and told the manager with her agreement, instead of letting her push through.

qa.q: How might Chetan have felt watching the monthly pain get worse?
qa.a: Worried and helpless, which is why he insisted this time.

grounding: Shows monthly pain and distress that disrupts work and relationships being brought to a doctor instead of being tolerated.

passage: Every month, in the week before her period, Sarika's life in their Kochi flat seemed to fall apart. She cried through meetings, snapped at Joseph over nothing, and one month called in sick three days running because she couldn't face anyone. Her mother said, 'All women go through it. Bear it.' Sarika had borne it for years. One evening, after a week of barely sleeping, she told Joseph, 'It feels like I disappear for a week and a stranger lives here.' Joseph held her hand. 'This isn't something you just tolerate. Let's see a doctor.' He found a women's health clinic, went with her, and helped her write down her monthly notes. The doctor took her seriously and made a plan with her.

qa.q: What did Sarika's mother say?
qa.a: 'All women go through it. Bear it.'

qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and lost, as if she disappeared for a week every month.

qa.a: He refused to treat it as something to tolerate, found a clinic, went with her and helped write down her monthly notes.
